title: INT 00h to INT 3Fh, the PC interrupt vectors
covers: The interrupt vectors of the IBM PC, 00h to 3Fh: what each one is, and what DOSBox-X does with it.

rows.text: Vector 00h is the CPU-generated divide error.
The CPU generates it when the divisor of a DIV or IDIV instruction is zero or the quotient overflows the result register.
An 8086 or 8088 raises it when the result of a division is 80h (byte) or 8000h (word).
Vector 01h is the CPU-generated single step; on the 80386 and later it is also the debugging exception.
The CPU generates it after each instruction if TF (trap flag) is set; TF is cleared on invoking the single-step handler.
Vector 02h is the non-maskable interrupt, generated by external hardware.
The CPU enters it when the input to the NMI pin is asserted.
On the PCjr the keyboard raises an NMI instead of IRQ1.
Vector 03h is the CPU-generated breakpoint.
The CPU generates it for the one-byte breakpoint instruction (opcode CCh).
Vector 04h is INTO detecting an overflow.
The INTO instruction generates it when OF (the overflow flag) is set; otherwise INTO is effectively a NOP.
Vector 05h is PRINT SCREEN; on the 80186 and later it is also the BOUND range exceeded exception.
It dumps the current text screen to the first printer.
It is normally invoked by the INT 09 handler when the PrtSc key is pressed.
BOUND calls it when the value tested is below the lower bound or above the upper bound.
The BIOS installs an IRET as the INT 05 handler.
No screen dump happens: the handler the BIOS installs does nothing unless hooked.
An application may invoke it directly.
Vector 06h is the CPU-generated invalid opcode exception.
The CPU raises it when it attempts an invalid opcode, or a BOUND, LDS, LES or LIDT instruction that names a register rather than memory.
Vector 07h is the CPU-generated processor extension not available exception.
The CPU calls it automatically when a coprocessor instruction is met and no coprocessor is installed.
Vector 08h is IRQ0, the system timer; on the 80286 and later it is also CPU-generated.
Channel 0 of the 8254 system timer generates it 18.2 times per second.
It is used to keep the time-of-day clock updated.
Programs that need to be invoked regularly should use INT 1C unless they need to reprogram the timer while keeping the time-of-day clock running at its proper rate.
The BIOS installs an IRQ0 callback whose stub issues INT 1Ch.
Vector 09h is IRQ1, the keyboard data ready interrupt; on the 80286 and 80386 it is also CPU-generated.
The CPU enters it when data is received from the keyboard: normally a scan code, or an ACK or NAK of a command on AT keyboards.
The BIOS installs its keyboard IRQ1 handler at vector 09h.
The keyboard raises IRQ1 when data is set at port 60, but on the PCjr the same data raises the NMI instead.
Vector 0Ah is IRQ2: LPT2 on the PC, the vertical retrace interrupt on the EGA and VGA, and IRQ9.
On ATs and above, the physical data line for IRQ2 is labeled IRQ9 and connects to the slave 8259.
The BIOS points vector 71h at a stub that issues INT 0Ah.
The BIOS redirects the interrupt for IRQ9 back to this vector.
Vector 0Bh is IRQ3, serial communications (COM2).
The UART automatically asserts it when COM2 needs attention, if the UART has been programmed to generate interrupts.
The BIOS installs its default IRQ handler at vector 0Bh.
Vector 0Ch is IRQ4, serial communications (COM1).
The UART automatically asserts it when COM1 needs attention, if the UART has been programmed to generate interrupts.
The BIOS installs its default IRQ handler at vector 0Ch.
Vector 0Dh is IRQ5: the fixed disk on the PC and XT, LPT2 on the AT, reserved on the PS/2.
The BIOS installs its default IRQ handler at vector 0Dh.
The default handler masks the line that raised the interrupt and acknowledges the PIC.
Vector 0Eh is IRQ6, the diskette controller.
The floppy disk controller generates it on completion of an operation.
The BIOS installs its floppy IRQ6 handler at vector 0Eh.
Vector 0Fh is IRQ7, the parallel printer.
The BIOS installs its default IRQ handler at vector 0Fh.
The default handler masks the line that raised the interrupt and acknowledges the PIC.
Vector 10h is the video interrupt; on the 80286 and later it is also the coprocessor error.
On the 80286 and later the CPU generates it when the -ERROR pin is asserted by the coprocessor.
The video BIOS installs its handler at vector 10h.
Vector 11h is the BIOS equipment list call; on the 80486 and later it is also CPU-generated.
It returns the BIOS equipment list word in (E)AX.
The BIOS installs its equipment list handler at vector 11h.
With a Weitek coprocessor enabled, bit 24 of EAX is set as well as the equipment word.
Vector 12h is the BIOS memory size call.
It returns in AX the kilobytes of contiguous memory starting at absolute address 00000h.
The BIOS installs its memory size handler at vector 12h.
Vector 13h is the disk interrupt.
The BIOS installs its disk handler at vector 13h.
Vector 14h is the serial interrupt.
The BIOS installs its serial port handler at vector 14h.
Vector 15h is the cassette interrupt.
The BIOS installs its system services handler at vector 15h.
Vector 16h is the keyboard get keystroke call.
Function 00h returns the next keystroke's BIOS scan code in AH and its ASCII character in AL.
The BIOS installs its keyboard handler at vector 16h.
Vector 17h is the printer BIOS call.
Function 00h writes character AL to printer DX and returns the printer status in AH.
The BIOS installs its printer handler at vector 17h.
Vector 18h is the diskless boot hook, called when no bootable disk is available.
Very few PCs other than IBM's contain BASIC in ROM, so on compatibles it often reboots the system.
The BIOS installs its diskless boot handler at vector 18h.
Vector 19h is the BIOS bootstrap loader: it reboots without clearing memory or restoring the interrupt vectors.
Usually the BIOS reads sector 1, head 0, track 0 from drive A: to 0000h:7C00h, and if that fails it reads the same sector of the first hard disk.
The BIOS installs its bootstrap loader at vector 19h.
DOSBox-X performs a software CPU reset and never reads a boot sector to 0000h:7C00h itself.
Vector 1Ah is the time BIOS call.
Function 00h returns the clock tick count since midnight in CX:DX and the midnight flag in AL.
The BIOS installs its time handler at vector 1Ah.
Vector 1Bh is the keyboard control-break handler.
The keyboard handler calls it when it determines that Control-Break was pressed.
The handler normally points at a short DOS routine that sets the Ctrl-C flag.
The BIOS installs a break handler at vector 1Bh and the DOS kernel replaces it with its own.
Vector 1Ch is the system timer tick.
The timer interrupt handler calls it automatically on each clock tick.
The BIOS installs its timer tick handler at vector 1Ch.
Vector 1Dh points at the video parameter tables.
In a 100% compatible BIOS the vector points at the parameter table at F000h:F0A4h.
DOSBox-X allocates the video parameter table in its ROM area and points the vector at that address.
Vector 1Eh points at the diskette parameters.
In a 100% compatible BIOS the default parameter table is located at F000h:EFC7h.
If the table is changed, INT 13/AH=00h should be called so the controller is reprogrammed.
DOSBox-X allocates the parameter table in its ROM area and points the vector at that address.
The DOS kernel copies the table's first 11 bytes to 0000h:0522 and points the vector there.
Vector 1Fh points at the 8x8 graphics font.
The vector points at 1024 bytes of graphics data, 8 bytes for each character 80h-FFh.
Vector 20h is the DOS terminate-program call.
It is equivalent to INT 21/AH=00h, which sets the program's return code to 00h.
The DOS kernel installs its terminate handler at vector 20h.
Vector 21h is the DOS function call interface.
The DOS kernel installs its function dispatcher at vector 21h.
Vector 22h is the address DOS returns to when a program terminates.
It should never be called directly, since it does not point at an interrupt handler.
During termination the vector is restored from the DWORD at offset 0Ah of the PSP and a FAR JMP is made to it.
When a program is loaded, DOSBox-X sets vector 22h to the caller's return address.
Vector 23h is the DOS Control-C and Control-Break handler.
DOS invokes it whenever it detects a Control-C or Control-Break.
The shell installs its own Control-C handler at vector 23h.
Vector 24h is the DOS critical error handler.
It should never be called directly.
When DOS terminates a program it copies the previous vector out of the PSP into the interrupt vector table.
DOSBox-X saves the vector in the PSP and restores it when the program ends.
The shell points vector 24h at a far jump back to the previous handler.
Vector 25h is the DOS absolute disk read call.
It reads CX sectors starting at logical sector DX of drive AL into the buffer at DS:BX.
The DOS kernel installs its absolute disk read handler at vector 25h.
Vector 26h is the DOS absolute disk write call.
It writes CX sectors starting at logical sector DX of drive AL from the buffer at DS:BX.
The DOS kernel installs its absolute disk write handler at vector 26h.
Vector 27h is the DOS terminate-and-stay-resident call.
It terminates the program, never returns, and keeps the number of bytes in DX resident.
INT 22, INT 23 and INT 24 are restored from the PSP.
The DOS kernel installs its terminate-and-stay-resident handler at vector 27h.
Vector 28h is the DOS idle interrupt.
DOS invokes it each time one of its character input functions loops while waiting for input.
The DOS kernel installs its idle handler at vector 28h, or a bare IRET when the idle api is off.
Vector 29h is the fast console output call.
It writes the character in AL to the console and returns nothing.
The DOS kernel installs a console output handler at vector 29h.
Vector 2Ah is the network installation check.
Function 00h returns AH nonzero if a network is installed.
The DOS kernel installs its network handler at vector 2Ah.
DOSBox-X's handler returns at once, leaving AH unchanged, so it never reports a network.
Vector 2Bh is reserved.
In MS-DOS 6.22 and earlier the vector is not used.
It points at an IRET instruction.
DOSBox-X points every vector below 60h at a default handler that returns.
Vector 2Ch is reserved.
In DOS 6.00 and earlier this vector points at an IRET instruction.
DOSBox-X points this vector, with every vector below 60h, at a default callback whose stub returns with an IRET.
Vector 2Dh is reserved.
In DOS 6.00 and earlier this vector points at an IRET instruction.
DOSBox-X points vector 2Dh at an AMIS handler that answers AH/AL calls and reports a free multiplex number, instead of leaving it at an IRET.
Vector 2Eh passes a command to the command interpreter for execution.
The caller gives DS:SI the address of the command line to execute.
The call destroys all registers except CS:IP.
It runs COMMAND.COM's internal commands without loading another copy of COMMAND.COM.
The command line is a count byte, the command string, and a terminal carriage return.
DOSBox-X returns with AX=0000h, CS:IP restored and SS:SP changed, and the other registers as the executed command left them.
Vector 2Fh is the multiplex interrupt: AH names the program that handles the call and AL is its function code.
AH 00h-3Fh is IBM's for DOS, 40h-7Fh Microsoft's, 80h-B7h IBM's, B8h-BFh the networks' and C0h-FFh the applications'.
It is a general mechanism for verifying that a TSR is present and for communicating with it.
When searching for a free AH the caller should set BX, CX and DX to 0000h and rely on no register but CS:IP and SS:SP.
A TSR that chains by calling the previous handler should preserve and pass back the flags.
DOSBox-X installs a multiplex handler at vector 2Fh that offers each call to the handlers registered with it.
INT 30h is not a vector: it is the far jump instruction the CALL 5 entry point jumps to.
The CALL 5 entry point does a far jump to this address.
In its default CP/M mode DOSBox-X's CALL 5 entry does a far call to 0000:00C0 or to its HMA mirror F01D:FEF0, where the far jump stands.
DOSBox-X installs the far jump to its CP/M handler at DOS startup, saving vectors 30h and 31h first.
Vector 31h is overwritten by the CP/M jump instruction in INT 30.
DOSBox-X saves vectors 30h and 31h before the jump overwrites 31h, and restores both when the DOS object is destroyed.
Vector 32h has no special use.
The list records viruses that keep the original INT 21h vector at 32h.
DOSBox-X leaves vector 32h at its default callback instead of a virus vector.
DOSBox-X points vector 32h at its default callback.
Vector 33h is the mouse driver interface; AX=0000h resets the driver and reads its status.
The reset returns FFFFh in AX when the driver is installed and 0000h when it is not, and the button count in BX.
On old machines the caller should first check that the vector is neither 0000h:0000h nor an IRET stub.
On a Hercules-compatible card in graphics mode the caller must first set 0040h:0049h to 6 for page 0 or 5 for page 1.
DOSBox-X returns FFFFh in AX and the button count in BX when the driver is present, and leaves both as they were when it is not.
DOSBox-X installs its INT 33h mouse callback at vector 33h when the int33 emulation is enabled, and skips it otherwise.
Vector 34h is the floating point emulation interrupt for instructions with opcode D8h.
The floating point emulators of Borland's and Microsoft's languages and of Lahey FORTRAN use this interrupt.
DOSBox-X leaves this vector at its default callback.
Vector 35h is the floating point emulation interrupt for instructions with opcode D9h.
The floating point emulators of Borland's and Microsoft's languages and of Lahey FORTRAN use this interrupt.
DOSBox-X leaves this vector at its default callback.
Vector 36h is the floating point emulation interrupt for instructions with opcode DAh.
The floating point emulators of Borland's and Microsoft's languages and of Lahey FORTRAN use this interrupt.
DOSBox-X leaves this vector at its default callback.
Vector 37h is the floating point emulation interrupt for instructions with opcode DBh.
The floating point emulators of Borland's and Microsoft's languages and of Lahey FORTRAN use this interrupt.
DOSBox-X leaves this vector at its default callback.
Vector 38h is the floating point emulation interrupt for instructions with opcode DCh.
The floating point emulators of Borland's and Microsoft's languages and of Lahey FORTRAN use this interrupt.
DOSBox-X leaves this vector at its default callback.
Vector 39h is the floating point emulation interrupt for instructions with opcode DDh.
The floating point emulators of Borland's and Microsoft's languages and of Lahey FORTRAN use this interrupt.
DOSBox-X leaves this vector at its default callback.
Vector 3Ah is the floating point emulation interrupt for instructions with opcode DEh.
The floating point emulators of Borland's and Microsoft's languages and of Lahey FORTRAN use this interrupt.
DOSBox-X leaves this vector at its default callback.
Vector 3Bh is the floating point emulation interrupt for instructions with opcode DFh.
The floating point emulators of Borland's and Microsoft's languages and of Lahey FORTRAN use this interrupt.
DOSBox-X leaves this vector at its default callback.
Vector 3Ch is the floating point emulation interrupt for instructions with a segment override.
The floating point emulators of Borland's and Microsoft's languages and of Lahey FORTRAN use this interrupt.
The generated code is CD 3C xy mm, and xy appears to encode the segment override in its ss bits as DS, SS, CS or ES.
DOSBox-X leaves vector 3Ch at its default callback.
DOSBox-X points vector 3Ch at its default callback.
Vector 3Dh is the floating point emulation interrupt for a standalone FWAIT.
The floating point emulators of Borland's and Microsoft's languages and of Lahey FORTRAN use this interrupt.
DOSBox-X points vector 3Dh at its default callback.
Vector 3Eh is Borland's floating point emulation shortcut call.
The two bytes after the instruction are the subcode and a NOP, except for subcodes DCh and DEh, where the second is a register count.
DOSBox-X leaves vector 3Eh at its default callback.
DOSBox-X points vector 3Eh at its default callback.
Vector 3Fh is the overlay manager interrupt used by Microsoft's LINK.EXE and Borland's TLINK VROOMM.
It is the default vector, and the linker may override it.
DOSBox-X points vector 3Fh at its default callback.
